1:
Jerome reads the verse as a joint: after the preaching and the teaching an occasion of working miracles is offered, so that by the mighty works which follow the doctrine that went before might be confirmed. Pseudo-Chrysostom gives that sequence a motive — because he had taught as one having authority, and such a manner of teaching might otherwise be put down to ostentation, he does in works what he had done in words. Clarke and Gill both identify the mountain as the one he had gone up into to preach the three preceding chapters, and Clarke has the crowds following because they had been deeply impressed by the doctrines they had just heard.

Henry works the crowd. The people astonished at his doctrine were loth to disperse, strict a Lawgiver and faithful a Reprover as he was; from which he draws the note that those to whom Christ has manifested himself cannot but desire to be better acquainted with him, and that they who know much of him should covet to know more. He sees Jacob’s prophecy of the Messiah fulfilled, that unto him shall the gathering of the people be — then withdraws half of it, since they who gathered did not cleave to him, and they who followed closely and constantly were few beside the multitudes who were followers at large. He explains too why the leper stands first among the miracles: leprosy was reckoned a particular mark of God’s displeasure, Miriam and Gehazi and Uzziah having each been struck with it for one particular sin.

Ellicott takes the arrangement as a problem rather than a sequence. Setting the three Gospels side by side he finds these events in three different orders, which is enough to show how hard it is to harmonise the narratives with certainty; and he draws three conclusions he will call all but certain — that each record is independent, since neither Mark nor Luke would have departed so widely had they had Matthew before them; that all three derive from earlier records embracing a few acts or discourses each; and that direct evidence of the order is absent, each writer being left to a principle of grouping of his own.

Pseudo-Origen reads the descent itself. While he taught on the mount the disciples were with him, to whom it was given to know the secret things of the heavenly doctrine; those who now follow had been altogether unable to climb it, since men bowed under the burden of sin cannot reach the sublime mysteries. The coming down is a stooping to the infirmity and helplessness of the rest, in pity to their imperfections — though he will not flatter them, since some followed for renown, most for the doctrine, and some for cures or to have their wants supplied. Haymo turns the mount into heaven, which is called God’s throne: while the Lord sits there only the disciples come to him, because before he took our frailty upon him God was known only in Judaea, and when he came down from the height of his Divinity a great multitude of the nations followed. From that he takes a rule for teachers, that speech be regulated to what each hearer can receive — they ascend the mount in showing the perfect the more excellent precepts and come down in showing the weak the lesser ones, there being a time for teaching and a time for healing. On the mount he had cured souls and healed hearts; coming down, he heals bodies. Pseudo-Chrysostom draws the leper into the same figure, as one who could not ascend because he bore the burden of sin, the sin of our souls being a leprosy, so that the Lord came down from the height of heaven as from a mountain to purge the leprousness of our sin.
2:
What the disease was gets three accounts that do not quite agree. Clarke derives the Greek name from the word for a scale and describes dry white scurfy scales over the whole body or part of it, with violent itching and often great pain; the eastern form he calls so contagious that it infected garments and even houses, and incurable by any human means, so that among the Jews God alone was applied to and the cure always put down to his sovereign power. Ellicott notes that the word is Greek and not Hebrew in origin and has been used with varying extent of meaning, sometimes taking in elephantiasis or even cancer, and that even in the narrower sense Hippocrates gave it there were three kinds, the mealy, the white and the black. He traces its origin to the squalor of the Egyptian bondage, it being the botch or plague of Egypt, and notes that Egyptian legends of the Exodus had the Israelites expelled as lepers. Barnes divides the three kinds by the colour of the spots instead, white, black and red, and insists it is seated not in the skin but deep in the bones and marrow, so that a man might live thirty or fifty years with it and see himself dying piece-meal as the extremities fell away.

Gill places the meeting. It happened as soon as he came down and while he was still on the road, though Luke sets it in a certain city — one of the unwalled towns of Galilee, into which a leper might lawfully come, whereas from a walled town they might turn him out. Wesley adds that such diseases were seldom curable there by natural means, no more than palsies or lunacy, and guesses that the man had heard the Lord at a distance, since he might not mix with the people.

What his gesture amounted to is disputed. Calvin examines the verb and finds in it the outward mark of reverence commonly used among the Jews, the people of the East being the more given to such ceremonies, and reports that many therefore take it for a respectful salutation offered to a distinguished prophet rather than divine worship. Pseudo-Chrysostom will have none of that: the man did not ask as of a human physician but adored him as God, and since faith and confession together make a perfect prayer, he performed the work of faith in adoring and the work of confession in speaking. Haymo marks the order of it, that he began to adore before he made his suit, and puts into his mouth the precedent of Naaman the Syrian cleansed of old by the hand of Elisha. Henry has him worshipping as one clothed with Divine power.

On the condition itself the comment converges. Robertson observes that the leper never questioned the power but only the willingness, and borrows the remark that men more easily believe in miraculous power than in miraculous love; he parses the clause as an undetermined condition with a prospect of being determined, a hopeful doubt at worst. Chrysostom reads the same words for what they concede: the man said not, if thou wilt ask of God, nor, if thou wilt make adoration to God, but simply if thou wilt, and did not even say cleanse me, leaving the whole to him and so owning him Lord of all. Pseudo-Chrysostom locates the doubt elsewhere again — not in Christ’s readiness to every good work, which is beyond doubt, but in whether this particular cure would be expedient, since soundness of body is not good for every man; so the clause says, I believe thou willest whatever is good, but I do not know whether what I want is good. Henry turns it into a rule for approach: we cannot demand mercy as a debt but must humbly request it as a favour.
3:
That the touch was an offence is where the moderns begin. Barnes notes that to touch a leprous person was reckoned to make a man ceremonially impure, so that putting forth the hand declared the intention to cure and was a pledge that it had already taken place. Ellicott calls the act a proof at once of the will and the power, and argues that he did not fear becoming unclean by the contact and was therefore not under the law that forbade it; and notes that Mark adds the compassion. Pseudo-Chrysostom puts the legal point exactly: the letter was transgressed and the meaning was not, since the Law forbade the touch only because it could not prevent the toucher being defiled, and meant not that lepers should go unhealed but that those who touched them should not be polluted — so he was not polluted by touching the leprosy but purified the leprosy by touching it.

Chrysostom sets the scene against Elisha. He could have cleansed by a word, or by the bare will, and put out his hand instead to show that he was not subject to the Law and that to the pure nothing is impure; where Elisha kept the Law strictly and sent Naaman to wash in Jordan instead of going out to touch him, this is no servant healing but a Lord, whose hand the leprosy did not make unclean because the holy hand made the leprous body pure. He adds the moral, that only the leprosy of the soul, which is sin, deserves dread, the leprosy of the body being no bar to virtue. Lightfoot works the same ground from the priesthood: it is a wonder the priest who judged so creeping an infection was never hurt by it, and he sets Aaron beside Miriam, who bore the leprosy for the guilt they shared while he did not, and Uzziah, whose encroachment on the priesthood God confuted by no other means than this plague.

Jerome divides the answer in two and will not have it read as one clause. It is not I will cleanse thee, as he says most of the Latins think, but first the answer I will, matching the leper’s if thou wilt, and then the command be thou clean, matching his thou canst make me clean. Chrysostom finds the first word unparalleled, since nowhere else does Christ use it however signal the miracle, and reads it as confirming what the crowd and the man already thought of his power; even straightway, he says, is too slow a word for the speed of the deed. Damascenus, quoted in the same place, explains why anything was said at all: had the cure been worked in silence, nobody would have known by whose power it came, so that the will to heal was for the leper and the word for those who stood watching. Clarke hears in it the most sovereign authority, with no supplication of any power above his own.

Calvin carries the touch further than the cure. Because Christ holds a purity that repels all filth, touching neither polluted him nor made him a transgressor; and in taking our flesh he was united to one body with ourselves, descending as far as hell without contracting a stain, and taking away our impurities by sprinkling us with his holiness. He might have healed by the word alone, and added the hand to express compassion. Gill reads the gesture for three things at once, the grace that would touch so loathsome a creature, the unspotted holiness that could not be defiled by it, and the power that healed by a touch and a word together. Clarke makes the whole action a figure of the invisible hand that is felt by the most insensible heart and the inward word that is heard by the most deaf.
4:
Why silence was imposed draws four answers. Clarke argues from policy: had Christ declared himself Messiah so early the people would have proclaimed him King, and his refusal would have earned the hatred of the Jewish rulers and the jealousy of Rome, so that his preaching and his miracles must have been impeded. Wesley lists four motives and will not choose between them — to keep the multitude from thronging him, to fulfil the prophecy that he would not be ostentatious, to avoid being seized and made a king by force, and to enrage the chief priests and scribes no more than was unavoidable. Chrysostom rejects one explanation outright: some say the command was given lest malice should cast doubt on the cure, which he calls foolishly said, since the man was not so cured that his cleanness could be questioned. The reason is rather that Christ does not love ostentation; and where elsewhere he told a healed man to go and tell, the lesson there was a thankful heart, so that by this leper we learn not to covet empty honour and by the other not to be ungrateful. Hilary offers a quieter motive, that the healing might be sought rather than offered.

How far the silence reached is read more narrowly. Barnes limits the command to the interval before the man presented himself to the priest: the cure was wrought in Galilee, forty or fifty miles from Jerusalem, and his duty was to hasten there rather than delay in talk, the more so because the report might outrun him and a priest hostile to Jesus pronounce the whole thing an imposition. Wesley reads the words the same way, as meaning not until he had shown himself to the priest appointed to inquire into such cases. Gill agrees that concealment was neither possible nor intended before a multitude, and makes the counsel specific to the journey, lest out of ill will to Christ the priests refuse to pronounce him clean. Calvin is harder on the man than any of them. Some excuse him by supposing the prohibition was not serious but a spur to publish the more; Calvin holds instead that the full time was not yet come, and that for the disorderly display of his regard the leper deserves condemnation rather than praise, since obedience was the thanks that was wanted.

The errand to the priest is given its own reasons. Jerome finds three: humility, so that Christ might seem to defer to the priests; evidence, so that seeing the leper cleansed they might be saved if they believed and be left without excuse if they did not; and prudence, that he might not seem to infringe the Law as he was so often charged with doing. Lightfoot dwells on his sending the man there at all, since the priesthood by then was far fallen from its institution and its office, and draws the principle that corruption defiles a divine institution but does not extinguish it; he sets out the Rubric too, three beasts for the cleansing, a sacrifice for sin, one for transgression and a burnt-offering, with birds allowed to a poor man. Clarke itemises the offering as two living clean birds with cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop. Chrysostom turns the last clause against its hearers: a testimony to them means an accusation of them, and Christ said not the gift that I command but the gift that Moses commanded, handing them over to the Law and closing the mouths of the unjust, so that none could say he had usurped the honour of the priests. Hilary proposes another construction of the same words, that what Moses commanded is a testimony and not an effect; and Pseudo-Chrysostom suggests the oblation was ordered so that if they should afterwards try to put the man out he might answer that they had taken gifts on his cleansing.
5:
Gill has him simply returned from the Galilean journey to the town he had been living in, which is called his own city. On the rank the moderns agree: Barnes and Clarke both make a centurion the commander of a hundred men in the Roman armies, Barnes adding that Judaea was a Roman province where garrisons were kept to hold the people in subjection and that this man was probably a pagan by birth, while Ellicott notes that the title began as commander of a hundred and was afterwards used with a good deal more latitude. Calvin supposes the band under him was quartered at Capernaum as garrisons commonly were for a town’s protection, and remarks that the place, lying on the water, was the more dissolute. Henry makes the most of what the man was: a supplicant, a Gentile, a Roman and an officer, probably in command of the detachment stationed there, and for all that eminently godly — from which he takes the note that God has his remnant among all sorts of people, and that nobody will be able to plead his calling in the great day, or say that he would have been religious had he not been a soldier.

Whether the man came at all is the difficulty, and it is met the same way by three. Ellicott observes that here he is said to have come in person while Luke has him never coming at all, sending first the elders of the Jews and then his friends; he reads the two reports as differently aimed, Matthew keeping the miracle close to the teaching it led to and Luke writing after closer inquiry into the details. Calvin calls the discrepancy a mere trifle on which readers trip into making two miracles out of one, since there is no impropriety in saying that a man did what was done in his name and at his request. Wesley agrees and adds the grammar of it, that Hebrew very frequently ascribes to a man the thing done and the words spoken by his order — as Matthew has the mother of Zebedee’s children ask what Mark has the sons themselves ask, she being only their mouth — and guesses he came a little way and turned back, judging himself unworthy to come the whole; though from the dismissal at the end of the story Wesley thinks he came in person at last. Robertson notes only that the dative stands where the genitive absolute would lead one to expect otherwise.

The fathers read the setting. Chrysostom pairs the two suppliants, the leper meeting him as he came down from the mountain and the centurion as he entered Capernaum, and asks why neither went up the mountain to find him: not from any slackness, since the faith of both was fervent, but so as not to interrupt the teaching. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes the move itself for a mystery — having taught on the mount and cleansed the leper at its foot, he goes to Capharnaum, which is to say that after the purifying of the Jews he went to the Gentiles — and calls this centurion the first-fruits of the Gentiles, beside whose faith all the faith of the Jews was unbelief, since he had neither heard Christ teach nor seen the leper cleansed and believed on the report alone. Haymo reads the name of the town, the town of fatness or the field of consolation, as the Church gathered out of the Gentiles, filled with spiritual fatness and comforted about heavenly things under the troubles of the world. Remigius finds the number significant: a hundred is a perfect number, so the centurion stands for those Gentiles who believed first and were perfect in virtue, and his praying for his servant is the first-fruits of the Gentiles praying for the salvation of the whole Gentile world.
6:
Whether the sufferer was a son or a slave is settled by appeal to Luke. Gill grants the difficulty, since the Greek word more commonly means a son or a child, and then lets Luke decide it, who calls him expressly a servant; Ellicott reasons the same way, that the commoner sense is servant and that Luke’s stricter word for a slave fixes it; Robertson simply calls him the boy, a bedridden paralytic. Clarke enters a point of address rather than of diagnosis, that the word rendered Lord here should be given as Sir whenever a Roman is the speaker.

What ailed him is pressed harder than the text requires. Barnes admits the particular form of the palsy is not named and guesses at the painful kind that brings violent cramps and endangers life at once. Ellicott takes the words for grievous torment as pointing to sharper suffering than palsy commonly brings, and offers three possibilities — something like rheumatic fever, or tetanus, or the particular paralysis that numbs the muscles while leaving the nerves of sensation to sharp pain — citing a like case of paralysis with agonising pain from the books of Maccabees. Lightfoot works instead on the verb for lying: it is the word for a corpse laid out ready to be carried away, and so expresses the dominion of the disease, the sick man being moved only by others and unable to stir himself, next door to being carried out. Clarke hears the same force in it, a man laid all along and reduced to utter impotence by the torments that went with it.

That the master should care at all is what strikes most of them. Gill reads the concern both ways, as proof that the servant was faithful and obedient, since Luke says he was dear to him and highly valued, and as proof that the master was a good one, who would not put a sick servant out of doors but kept him at home and sought relief for him. Clarke sharpens it into a rebuke of his own day: many masters have an afflicted servant removed at once to an infirmary, often to a workhouse, or sent back to relatives who either care nothing for him or cannot afford him the comforts of life — which in a contagious case may be necessary, but not in common ones. Ellicott makes the pity itself the evidence, that such feeling was a mark of something exceptionally good in the man, since wealthy Romans did not for the most part deal so with their slaves when they fell sick. Rabanus hears the grief in the recital, that the man was sick, that it was palsy, that he was grievously afflicted, each clause added to show his own sorrow of heart and to move the Lord to mercy — and takes it for a pattern, that all ought so to feel for their servants and take thought for them. Chrysostom turns the same silence about bringing the sufferer into praise: some say the details were an excuse for leaving him behind, since a man in that state could not be carried, but he judges it a mark of faith greater even than that of the men who let a paralytic down through a roof, because one who knew a word would be enough thought it needless to bring him at all. Hilary reads the servant as a figure, the Gentiles being the sick of this world, their limbs unnerved and unfit for standing or walking, so that the salvation of the believing Gentiles is prefigured in him.
7:
The answer is read first for what it concedes. Gill calls it short and full, and notes that it offers more than was asked: the presence was never requested, and yet it is the presence that is promised, and not in the manner of an ordinary physician coming to see the case and do what he can, but a flat undertaking to heal. Chrysostom makes the same observation into a rule broken for once — Christ commonly follows the wish of the suppliant, but here he runs ahead of it, promising not only the cure but the visit, and does so that the centurion’s worth may be learnt. Jerome has him answering three things he had seen in the man at once, his faith in believing the Saviour able to heal, his humility in owning himself unworthy of a guest, and his thoughtfulness in discerning the Divinity under the covering of a body.

Clarke will not let the promise stand in the received form. Christ did not say he would come and heal, which could not have been strictly true since the cure was worked without his going to the house; the Greek is rather that he is coming and will heal, and taken so it holds a promise none of them distinctly understood — that foreseeing how the man’s faith would act, he would heal the servant on the way, before ever reaching the door, which is exactly what happened. Ellicott fills in the movement from Luke, where the words are not reported but are implied in his setting off with the elders of the synagogue: somebody seems to have run ahead with the news that the prayer was heard, and the centurion in his humility sent friends out with the message which this Gospel gives as though it came from his own lips. Robertson adds the verbs. The form is a plain future and not a question, and the word used here means first to serve or give medical attention and only then to cure, where the centurion and the narrator both reach for the more definite word for healing. He notes that Luke, writing as a physician, keeps the distinction when he says Jesus healed those who needed treatment, and keeps it again in the account of Malta, where one verb carries Paul’s miraculous cures and another what looks like the physician’s own practice — though he grants the distinction is not always observed. On the messengers he agrees with the others that two deputations carried the words which stand here in the centurion’s mouth.
8:
Who spoke the words is settled again from Luke. Gill has them delivered by friends in the centurion’s name once he learnt that Christ had agreed to come with the Jewish elders he had first sent, and had actually set out; conscious of his unworthiness, he deputed others to say this on the road. Wesley identifies them as a second set of messengers. Calvin holds that the concise report and the fuller one come to the same thing, and draws out two points in the speech: the man spares Christ by way of honouring him, asking him not to trouble himself because a visit is more than he deserves; and he credits him with power enough that a bare expression of his will should make the servant live. Ellicott supplies Luke’s opening words, trouble not thyself, and traces the verb from the idea of flaying or mangling to that of worrying and vexing.

The humility is weighed and found to be more than good manners. Barnes insists it points to a view of personal unworthiness rather than merely to being a Gentile, and reads in it a conviction of the Saviour’s dignity and power so strong that the man judged himself unfit to have the Son of God in his house — which he takes for the feeling proper to every penitent. Calvin finds the humility astonishing on the other side, since the man exalted so far above himself someone belonging to a conquered and enslaved nation, and guesses that long use of Jewish pretensions had made him content to be reckoned a heathen. Rabanus puts a scruple behind it: conscious of his Gentile life, he thought such condescension would burden him more than profit him, holding the faith but not yet initiated in the sacraments. Augustine turns the disclaimer inside out — by declaring himself unworthy he showed himself worthy, not of the house but of the heart, since he could not have spoken with such faith had he not already carried within him the one he feared to lodge; and it would have been no great blessedness to have Christ inside his walls had he not first entered the heart.

The request itself is read as the crux. Ellicott calls it the special proof of the man’s faith, since he had risen above any thought of an influence working by touch or charm to the thought of a power that needed only the will of the one who held it. Clarke prefers a reading supported by the widest evidence of manuscripts, versions and fathers, speak by word or command, and finds in the whole sentence the pattern of faith and humility that should attend a sinner’s prayer, since Christ can will away a palsy and speak away the worst torments; he grades the humility in two degrees, first owning the need of mercy and one’s own helplessness, then confessing the freeness of grace and one’s utter unworthiness, and names ignorance, unbelief and presumption as what retards the cure. Chrysologus reads the roof mystically as the body that houses the soul, and answers that God disdains neither to inhabit flesh nor to come under that roof. Pseudo-Origen applies the sentence to his own readers: when holy men who govern churches come under your roof the Lord comes in them, and when you eat and drink the Lord’s Body he comes under your roof indeed, so that the words are to be said then — for where he is received unworthily he enters to the receiver’s condemnation.
9:
The argument is a soldier’s and is read as such. Gill names the authority he stands under as Caesar’s and that of the officers above him, a tribune and the rest. Barnes sets out the reasoning in the man’s own form: being subject to orders he knows how to obey, and having men under him who are used to obeying, he is ready to believe that a command of Christ’s will be obeyed too — as his soldiers obey him, so do diseases and storms and seas obey the other; and if men obey an inferior officer who is himself under command, how much more shall diseases obey the original source of power. Wesley compresses the same step into a sentence, that what he orders is done even in his absence, and how much more what the Lord of all orders. Robertson hears an emphasis in the connecting word, even I in my subordinate place have soldiers under me, and observes that a military man had learnt obedience upwards and therefore expected it downwards, and instantly, which is why he could believe in a power over the boy’s illness exercised without a visit. Augustine states the inference bare: if one who is himself under command can yet command others, how much more he whom all powers serve.

Calvin enters a caution about the form of the argument, that the comparison asserts no equality between the two cases but runs from the less to the greater, the man conceiving the divine power in Christ as something higher than his own authority over servants and soldiers. Ellicott admires the reasoning for its artlessness and states the premise he thinks it rests on: experience had taught him that in any well ordered system a delegated authority can itself delegate, so that his own presence was needless where a soldier or a slave could be sent to act on his orders. Might he not argue from that analogy, Ellicott asks, to a kingdom in which one endued with power would likewise have ministers at hand — the unknown forces that govern life and death, whether personal or not he did not care to enquire — ready to execute his will? Hilary supplies the theological reason for his resting on a word, that the salvation of the Gentiles is all of faith and their life lies in the precepts of the Lord.

Two further readings turn the soldiers into something else. The Gloss puts the angels in their place: thou canst without thy bodily presence say to this disease, Go, by the ministry of thy angels, and it will leave him, and say to health, Come, and it will come to him. Haymo, quoted beside it, makes the men under command the natural virtues in which many of the Gentiles were strong, or else a man’s own thoughts good and bad — the bad to be told to depart, the good to be called, and the body, which is our servant, to be bidden submit itself to the will of God. Clarke, meanwhile, spends his space on the rank, granting that the verse has embarrassed commentators and critics and explaining the Roman foot by its three divisions, each of thirty companies, each company making two centuries of a hundred men with two centurions over them who were nowhere near equal in standing though their office was the same; the centurions of the two senior divisions were elected first and took precedence of those elected last, and he guesses this officer belonged to the junior sort.
10:
That Christ should marvel at all is the first difficulty. Gill confines the wonder to his manhood, since nothing could take God unawares or raise an admiration that cannot properly fall on a divine person, and suggests he behaved in word and gesture as astonished men do in order to raise the attention of those standing by. Calvin reasons the same way, that wonder arises from what is new and unexpected and so cannot touch God, but could exist in one who had clothed himself with our flesh and with human affections. Augustine presses it harder still: who had created this faith but the very one who now marvels at it, and how should he wonder who foreknows everything? When the Lord marvels, Augustine answers, it is to teach us what we ought to wonder at, these emotions in him being not signs of passion but a teacher’s examples. Ellicott takes the opposite line and keeps the surprise, finding in it something that bears on the reality of our Lord’s human consciousness, facts coming to him in that true humanity unlooked-for, as they come to other men. Chrysostom says he wondered in the hearing of the whole crowd on purpose, to give them an example of wondering at him too.

How the praise can be absolute is the second. Calvin denies that it is, and will not have it measured against every property of faith — by that measure Mary’s was greater, who believed she would conceive by the Holy Ghost and bear the only-begotten Son, and owned the son she had borne as her God and the Creator of the world and her only Redeemer. Pseudo-Chrysostom grades it by the believer instead: Andrew believed, but after the Baptist had pointed out the Lamb of God; Peter by reading the Scriptures; Nathanael after a proof of the Divinity had been given him. Every good in a man is commended relative to what he is, so that wisdom in a countryman is a great thing where in a philosopher it would be nothing wonderful. Wesley puts the limitation in six words, that the centurion was not an Israelite. Ellicott marks the contrast concretely: Israelites who came for healing wanted presence, or a touch, or grosser signs still, where this man believed in the power of the word and asked nothing else.

What the faith was worth is weighed last. Barnes takes the word for confidence that Christ could heal the servant, grants it need not amount to saving faith, but thinks from the spirit shown that it did, which would make the man the first Gentile convert and an early instance of what was revealed more plainly afterwards. Clarke gathers from Luke, where the centurion is said to have loved the nation and built them a synagogue, that he was a proselyte of the gate like the officer in Acts, believing in the God of Israel without taking on the ritual or circumcision; and though he calls the military life one of the worst nurses for religion, he notes that instances of real humility and faith have been found in soldiers of every nation. Augustine makes the same point by omission, that Christ praised the faith and gave no order to leave the profession. Pseudo-Origen asks what it is that the Only-begotten marvels at, and answers that gold and riches and principalities are to him a shadow or a fading flower, and faith alone is precious; and he sets three failures beside it — Jairus, a prince in Israel, who asked not for a word but for a quick journey; Nicodemus, who met the mystery with how can these things be; and the sisters at Bethany, who said that had he been there their brother would not have died, as though God’s power could not be in two places at once.
11:
That the saying is a digression is agreed. Gill has our Lord turning aside, on the occasion of this one Gentile’s faith, to the calling of the Gentiles at large, and reading the single case as what would shortly be fulfilled in great numbers of them, drawn from the rising of the sun to its setting and from the four corners of the earth. Barnes makes the same point and glosses the geography, since east and west in Scripture stand for the whole world, so that the conversion would not be a solitary one but would bring many of the heathen to be saved as the patriarchs were. Calvin arranges the two halves of the story: in the servant Christ gave the Gentiles a taste and a kind of first-fruits of his grace, and in the master he sets out the future calling of the nations and the spread of faith through the world, not from neighbouring countries only but from its farthest bounds. He adds what made this hard hearing, that the Jews imagined God confined to the family of Abraham and heard with astonishment that present strangers would be citizens and heirs. Ellicott sees in the centurion the first-fruits of the whole later harvest, and says that these words contain by implication the entire gospel Paul afterwards preached to the Gentiles.

The table is read for its posture and its promise. Clarke explains that sitting down means sitting down to meat, the word carrying the reclining posture the easterns used at meals, and notes that the rabbis themselves pictured the blessedness of the kingdom as a banquet; he takes the whole saying as spoken to soften Jewish prejudice and prepare them to receive the rest of mankind into fellowship. Barnes agrees that the enjoyments of heaven are commonly described under the figure of a feast and that the posture denotes honour, since to sit with such men was itself a distinction. Robertson adds that they reclined on couches, as Jews and Romans did, which makes the most famous painting of the Last Supper an anachronism with everyone seated in the modern way. Clarke enters one condition on the promise, that those who would inherit it must be followers of the men named in it.

The quarters of the compass are given further senses. Augustine notes that the word is not all but many, and that east and west between them are meant to take in the whole world. Haymo, quoted beside him, divides them instead: from the east come those who pass into the kingdom as soon as they are enlightened, from the west those who have borne persecution for the faith even to death. Jerome grounds the seating arrangement in the identity of the God concerned — because the God of Abraham, the Maker of heaven, is the Father of Christ, Abraham is himself in the kingdom, and the nations who believed in Christ the Son of the Creator will sit down with him. Wesley draws the sharp edge of it, that men from the farthest parts of the earth will take the terms and enjoy the rewards of the covenant made with Abraham, while the Jews, who had the first title to them, are shut out from the feast, from grace now and from glory afterwards. Ellicott observes that Luke omits these words altogether, and thinks the omission significant either way: if he did not know them, his record is wholly independent; if he did, then writing for Gentiles he may have preferred to leave them here and record them where our Lord repeated them later, repetition of that kind being entirely after his manner.
12:
Who the children of the kingdom are is not in dispute, but the title is. Gill explains the Jews held it on several grounds at once: they were subjects of the commonwealth of Israel from which the Gentiles were aliens, they stood in the church of God which is his kingdom on earth, they had the promise of the Gospel dispensation which they themselves commonly called the world to come, and they expected the kingdom of glory as heirs; he notes that son and children of the world to come are frequent phrases in their own writings. Barnes puts it as presumption, that they supposed themselves the particular favourites of heaven and looked for a Messiah who would enlarge the nation and spread its conquests, so that they used the title to shut the Gentiles out — and our Lord answered them in the very idiom they were used to. Ellicott calls the form a Hebraism, like the children of the bride-chamber, and adds the sting, that these were the natural heirs who had forfeited the inheritance. Robertson lists the parallel idioms, son of hell and sons of this age, and recalls that the Baptist had already denied that natural birth brings spiritual sonship. Calvin alone treats the name as a problem: how can men be called this who were aliens from the faith and so no part of God’s flock? His answer is that they held a place in the Church even without belonging to it, and that while the covenant stood in the family of Abraham it carried force enough for the heavenly inheritance to be theirs peculiarly, the later rejection itself proving they had belonged to the family at the time.

The darkness is read from the banquet. Clarke works out the figure in detail: salvation is set out here as a nuptial festival where the guests recline with the master of the feast, and since such solemnities were held at night the house of reception was filled with lights, the torches and lamps and candles and lanterns that Athenaeus and Plutarch name, so that those admitted had the benefit of the light and those shut out stood in the darkness outside. Ellicott makes the same contrast and insists on the article, that it is strictly the outer darkness, set against an interior blazing with lamps; and he notes that both of the following words carry the article too, the weeping being the weeping of all weeping, the pair of them occurring six times in this Gospel and once in Luke. Robertson reads the comparative as our further out, the darkness beyond the limits of the lighted palace, and finds the repeated article bolder still. Wesley mentions the same custom of feasting at night, and guesses that while the words were being spoken the centurion arrived in person. Barnes takes the image from a different quarter and thinks it not unlikely to be drawn from Roman dungeons.

Three readings press the punishment further. Jerome allows the title on the ground that God had reigned among them heretofore, and explains the epithet simply: the darkness is outer because the man whom the Lord casts out leaves the light behind him. Rabanus takes the gnashing for the passion of remorse, a repentance that comes too late and accuses itself of having sinned with such obstinate wickedness. Remigius turns the whole sentence into history rather than hell, making the outer darkness the foreign nations and the saying a prediction of the destruction of the Jews, who were to be carried into captivity for unbelief and scattered over the earth; and since tears come of heat and chattering teeth of cold, he assigns the weeping to those dispersed into the warm countries, India and Ethiopia, and the gnashing to those who should live in the cold ones, Hyrcania and Scythia.
13:
Gill marks only that the digression is over and the answer returned. On the measure named in it the comment turns practical. Clarke reads the clause as making the mercy equal to the faith brought to receive it, and takes according to thy faith be it done for a general rule of God’s dealings with men, so that to gain an increase of faith is to gain an increase of every grace; he holds that God is the same now as in ancient days and that cures of body and soul may still be wrought through the instrumentality of faith, and ends on the complaint that faith is hardly to be found. Calvin draws the same lesson from the other side: it is plain here how freely Christ pours out grace where he finds the vessel of faith open, and though the words are addressed to one man they invite everyone to strong hope — which tells us why God is for the most part so sparing with us, since it is our unbelief that will not let him be liberal. Rabanus states the proportion as a sentence of its own, that the grace is according to the measure of the faith, and adds that a master’s merit may reach his servants through their obedience and not only through faith of their own. Ellicott makes a small correction of tense, that it should be as thou didst believe, pointing back to the one great act, and reminds the reader that the words went as a message.

The cure itself raises the harmonising question. Barnes takes the healing in that selfsame hour as decisive of both the goodness and the power, a miracle so complete that no imposition or deception was possible, and then reports the dispute over whether Luke tells the same story at all, some holding that a second centurion, encouraged by the success of the first, came in a like case and got a like answer, and that the two accounts disagree too far to be reconciled. Chrysostom had already registered the same opinion and thought it had much to support it, pointing to the difference in what is said of each man — of the one in Luke, that he loved the nation and had built them a synagogue, and of this one, that such faith had not been found in Israel.
14:
Whose house it was gets worked out from the other Gospels. Gill makes it Andrew’s as well, the brothers living together, and places it at Capernaum, to which they had moved from Bethsaida after their call, though he suspects the house really belonged to the sick woman and was called theirs only because they lodged there. Clarke infers from a later chapter that Peter lived there and that Christ lodged with him. Ellicott adds from Mark and Luke that the day was a Sabbath and that our Lord had already taught in the synagogue and healed a demoniac, the four fishermen being present, so that the party came to the house when the service was over. Barnes notes what Mark supplies, that the brothers lived together, that the sons of Zebedee came too, and that they spoke to him about the sick woman before the cure. Robertson reads the two participles for her state, bedridden and burning, remarks that nobody tells us what kind of fever it was or how long it had held her, and observes that fever was itself reckoned a disease, the English word coming from the same root as fire, like the Greek.

That a married apostle is mentioned here draws comment out of all proportion. Barnes argues from the phrase that Peter either was or had been married and thinks the obvious reading is that his wife was then living, with Paul for a witness. Clarke borrows Theophylact to say that marriage is no hindrance to virtue since the chief of the apostles had a wife, and presses it into an argument: marriage is among the first of the divine institutions, God himself having said the single state is not good, so that those who claim celibacy is the holier slander their Maker and say in effect that they are too holy to keep his commandments. Ellicott grants the point and checks the use made of it, calling the fact of Peter’s marriage almost unduly prominent in the Protestant case against enforced celibacy. Wesley says only that Peter was then a young man, as all the apostles were.

Why Christ entered at all, and where the episode belongs, divide the fathers from the harmonists. Chrysostom thinks he went in to take food, since she rose and ministered to them, and that he visited his disciples to honour them and make them the more zealous; he also admires Peter’s restraint, that with his wife’s mother lying in a fever at home he neither hurried Christ there nor brought him, but waited until the teaching was done and others healed, having been trained from the first to prefer others to himself — so that the entry, coming unasked, shows what is granted to a disciple where even the centurion had thought himself unworthy of it. He notes too that Mark adds the word immediately and reports that the sick woman was entreated for, where this Gospel gives the miracle bare, and calls the difference one of brevity against exact narrative rather than of disagreement. Augustine refuses to fix the time at all: Matthew has not said what this followed, and may be returning to something omitted earlier, since Mark puts it after the cleansing of the leper and Luke follows Mark, both setting it before the long sermon — and he asks what it matters in what order events are told. Henry reports the harmonists’ verdict, that this passage and all that follows to the end of the next chapter belongs before the sermon, with Lightfoot moving only this part of it; and he reads the case itself as deliberately ordinary, fevers being the commonest of distempers, recorded because the patient was a near relation of a disciple and so an instance of Christ’s kindness to the families of his own.
15:
The manner of the cure is noted before its effect. Gill ranges it among the others, since Christ healed the centurion’s servant by a word, this woman by a touch, and the leper by both; and he borrows from Luke that he stood over her, reached across to take her hand and lift her, and rebuked the fever as he afterwards rebuked the winds and the sea, having diseases at his command as he had the elements. Robertson reads the touch as loving sympathy, the Great Physician doing what any good doctor does, and finds in the following verb the beginning of a service taken up at table at once, out of gratitude. Clarke asks what short of unlimited power could work such a cure by a touch, and holds that even if the Scriptures had never spoken of Christ’s divinity these proofs must have demonstrated it to any man not blinded beforehand by his creed; he also prefers, on the weight of manuscripts, versions and fathers, that she ministered to him rather than to them, and makes the service a pattern, since to serve Christ in his ordinances and his members is the best evidence of a soul soundly restored.

The ministering is read as part of the miracle rather than a sequel to it. Ellicott takes it for proof of how complete the work was, the great fever having left behind none of its usual weakness and exhaustion. Jerome states the medical expectation it defeats: weakness naturally follows a fever, and a patient feels the evils of sickness as he begins to recover, whereas health given by the Lord’s power is whole from the first moment. The Gloss makes the same point as an addition rather than an absence, that it was not enough for her to be cured but strength was given her besides. Bede finds in the touched hand the turning of carnal works to spiritual uses, Rabanus the soul that struggled with fleshly lusts now bridling them by continence and serving righteousness with the very limbs that had served uncleanness, and Hilary the unbelief cured in Peter’s house, which is the body, so that it waits on the Saviour in duties of righteousness.
16:
Why the hour is given divides them. Gill rejects two common explanations — that the cool of the evening suited such a climate better than the heat of the day, and that the time was inconvenient and the cures therefore a mark of compassion in one already wearied — and holds that the real reason is the Sabbath, which their own canons would not let them anticipate. Clarke agrees and cites the rabbinic rule that the Sabbath does not begin until the sun is set, so that the sick could not be carried out before. Barnes makes the same point, that on the Sabbath they would not so much as bring their sick. Ellicott allows both reasons at once, the heat of the afternoon and the scruple that made Pharisees question whether a man might carry the bed he had lain on, so that with sunset the friends of the sick felt free to act. Lightfoot describes how the day was closed, at a supper where a candle and wine and spices were used as at its opening, with a blessing said over the cup, then the candle, then the spices. Augustine fastens on the exact wording, that it means the evening of that same day and would not have implied it had the phrase stood alone.

How the Evangelist handles so many cures at once is the next remark. Chrysostom observes that the crowd of believers was by now too great to disperse though the hour pressed, and that the writer runs through an innumerable flood of miracles without giving a single case, putting the whole in a word; and he explains the quotation that follows as a guard against the unbelief such a number might provoke, a prophet being brought in to witness what was done. Robertson keeps the scene instead, a sunset at the close of the Sabbath, the whole town gathered at the door of Peter’s house with those who had it badly, cured with a word — a thing those who saw it never forgot. Barnes draws an argument from the indiscriminate healing: everyone brought was cured, which proves both the benevolence and the commission, since he might have proved the latter by wonders that did nobody any good, and in fact worked none for display, unless the withered fig-tree be counted an exception.

The demoniacs and the hour both get further handling. Clarke, borrowing from Lightfoot, gives two reasons why Judaea then swarmed with the possessed, the first being that the nation had risen to the very height of impiety, for which he calls their own historian as witness that no people under heaven was more wicked. Remigius keeps to the manner of the cures, that the source of all goodness furnished a heavenly medicine and dismissed devils and diseases alike with a word, showing by such works that he had come for the saving of the race, and took the infirmity of our nature on himself to make the weak strong. Jerome reads the timing as a sign, that the healings came neither in the morning nor at noon but towards sunset, as a grain of wheat dies in the ground to bring forth much fruit. Rabanus takes the same sunset for the passion and death of the one who called himself the light of the world while he was in it, who taught only a few of the Jews during his life in the flesh but, having trodden down the kingdom of death, promised the gifts of faith to the Gentiles everywhere.
17:
Everyone notices that the prophecy is being used in an unexpected sense. Barnes insists the Greek renders the Hebrew exactly and that the English should have been the same in both places, and argues that the word given as griefs in Isaiah and infirmities here properly means diseases of the body in both tongues, referring in neither to sin or to sickness of mind — so that although Isaiah states the doctrine of atonement fully in that chapter, in this particular verse he states just what Matthew says he does. Clarke goes the other way: the Hebrew verb means to bear sin so as to make atonement for it, and the rabbis themselves took the place for the Messiah’s sufferings on behalf of Israel, holding that all her diseases and griefs and punishments should be borne by him; the prophecy properly concerns the taking away of sin and the Evangelist applies it to the removal of bodily afflictions. Calvin states the difficulty at its sharpest, that the prediction looks inappropriate and even tortured, Isaiah speaking of a death and of eternal grace where Matthew speaks of miracles and temporal benefits; his solution is that the Evangelist gives not merely the benefit those sick people received but the purpose for which the diseases were healed, so that the design and not the passing advantage is what must be looked at.

Wesley resolves it by degrees of meaning. The prophet spoke in a more exalted sense and the Evangelist only alludes to words that will carry this lower one as well, which he calls an elegance rather than an imperfection and frequent in the sacred writings: the highest fulfilment was the bearing of our sins in his own body on the tree, the lower a sympathy in our sorrows and the healing of diseases that were sin’s fruit. Ellicott finds the citation valuable precisely as a specimen of this Evangelist’s method with Messianic prophecy, and will not let the lower sense be slight: the writer, with that evening in his memory, saw the words fulfilled in the lifting of infirmities from men’s bodies, and the point is that he did not scatter relief as a rich man scatters alms but himself took and bore what he removed. Rabanus puts the same distinction in a phrase, that he took them not to keep them but to take them from us, and bore what we were too weak to bear; and Hilary carries it to the passion, where he absorbed all the infirmities of human weakness.

Robertson canvasses the translators without settling the matter, reporting renderings that make the sense a taking away of sickness and a carrying of the burden of disease, and Deissmann’s view that the Evangelist interpreted the Hebrew freely, set the Septuagint aside and transposed the two verbs, so that the meaning is a taking of our pains upon himself and a bearing of our diseases; Plummer he quotes for the opinion that the question is both impossible and unnecessary to settle. Lightfoot supplies what none of the others do, that the Talmudists drew a name for the Messiah out of this very verse, calling him the leper of the house of Rabbi because he bore our infirmities, and that some were content to reckon Rabbi Judah the Holy a candidate for the title on the strength of the many sicknesses he endured.
18:
Where he was going is quickly settled. Barnes places him at Capernaum, on the north-west corner of the lake, making for the country on its eastern side; Clarke names the lake and the Gergesene territory beyond it; Ellicott marks the eastern shore and detects behind the order, less plainly here than in the other Gospels, a longing for rest and retirement. Wesley says the same in a line, that both he and the people might have a little rest. Calvin dissents on the geography: the phrase need not mean the strictly opposite shore but the curve of the lake below Capernaum, so that he crossed to another part of it without leaving Galilee at all. Calvin also notes what this Gospel omits and the others supply, that he withdrew privately before daylight for solitude, and that Peter came to tell him the crowds were looking for him.

Why he left when he did is read as the real question, and the answers run opposite ways. Gill sorts the crowd by motive and finds little to admire: some came out of curiosity to see the man they had heard of, some to see miracles, some for the cure of their bodies, and few if any to hear the Gospel or for the good of their souls, the greater part coming with carnal and selfish ends. Chrysostom reads the departure as a lesson in doing nothing for display, since one who purified souls as well as healing bodies would show true wisdom by declining a crowd; and he observes the tact of it, that Christ did not dismiss the multitudes and so offend them, but told his disciples to cross, leaving the crowds free to hope they might follow. Remigius agrees that he meant to escape the thronging, and then turns to the crowd’s side of it: who would willingly leave a man who did such works, or not wish to look on that face and the mouth that spoke such things? If the countenance of Moses was made glorious and Stephen’s shone like an angel’s, he says, let the reader gather from that how their common Lord must have appeared, of whom it was written that his form is fair above the sons of men.

Henry takes the move for a principle of ministry rather than a retreat. The influences of this Sun of righteousness were not to be kept to one place but spread over the whole country, and the necessities of souls elsewhere were a call to come over and help them; so that his being welcome and useful where he stood was no reason to stay, since others were as eager to have him and must have their share. The departure is ordered, Henry notes, at the very moment when the multitudes about him showed how much they wanted him there. He also has the disciples’ own boats waiting, so that the command was to get their vessels ready for the crossing.
19:
What the man was is agreed and what he wanted is not. Gill places the exchange on the road down to the shore, as they went to take ship. Clarke suspects the singular is meant literally rather than as a Hebraism, to mark how few of that class ever came to Christ for instruction or salvation, and corrects the address to teacher, from a verb that properly means to show, so that the title belongs to one who points out a way. Robertson agrees the man was a disciple already, since the next applicant is called another of the disciples, but calls him a bumptious brother full of self-confidence, borrowing the remark that he came from the least impressionable class of all, in spirit utterly opposed to the ways of Jesus — and notes that he is nevertheless dealt with gently. Ellicott takes the opposite view of the same fact and finds it striking that a scribe should come at all, since it shows the teaching had reached beyond the common people who heard him gladly; as Nicodemus had owned him a teacher come from God, so here was a man whom the Sermon on the Mount or some like discourse had moved to volunteer at least the appearance of discipleship.

The offer is weighed against the answer it drew. Barnes thinks it not improbable that the man, having seen the miracles, expected some considerable worldly advantage from following, so that the reply proclaimed Christ’s poverty and dashed an avaricious hope: foxes and birds have shelter where the Son of man has neither home nor pillow, a stranger in his own world. Jerome makes the fault lie in the address itself, holding that the man would not have been turned away had he said Lord, and that because he reckoned the Saviour one master among many and was a man of the letter rather than a spiritual hearer, there was no place in him where Christ might lay his head; and he too supposes the miracles and the gain to be had from them were the attraction, which puts the scribe in the position of Simon Magus offering Peter money. Clarke draws the general moral, that a man not illuminated by the Spirit thinks himself capable of anything, where one divinely taught knows he can do nothing except as Christ strengthens him.

Two further readings concern the form of the approach. Hilary first widens the word disciples beyond the Twelve, there being many others, and then finds the flaw in the question rather than the motive: a doctor of the Law asks whether he should follow, as though the Law did not already say whom it were gain to follow, and so betrays unbelief under the diffidence of an enquiry — faith being taken up not by asking but by following. Calvin sets the two applicants side by side with the three in Luke, all of them ready to be disciples and all held back by some different fault, so that each gets a different answer; he grants it looks strange that the man offering to come at once is sent away while the one asking for a delay is kept, and locates the reason in what the eager man had failed to reckon with, namely how hard and wretched the condition was that he was volunteering for.
20:
The answer is taken first as a statement of fact about his condition. Calvin has him describing what his life on earth actually was and at the same time telling his disciples what to expect, and admits the oddity of the claim, since godly and generous people would gladly have taken him in; the words are a warning to this applicant in particular, not to look for rich wages from a master who lives himself on a precarious subsistence in borrowed houses. Gill has Christ answering what he saw in the man’s heart, the carnal and worldly views he came with. Ellicott thinks the reply implies the discipleship was hardly more than a show, the man having counted no cost, like the ruler with great possessions; to follow the Son of Man was not to join a new sect or serve a king marching to an earthly throne but to share poverty and homelessness. Wesley draws the practical conclusion in a clause, that nobody should follow him with a view to temporal advantage.

The words themselves are examined closely. Robertson glosses the first as a lurking burrow and denies that the second means nests at all, preferring leafy roosts where birds settle for the night, and notes that the same Greek word is used in the Greek Old Testament of God tabernacling in the sanctuary. Ellicott makes a smaller version of the same correction, that nest will do for popular use but strictly belongs only to the brooding season, where the Greek carries the wider sense of shelter. On the title both mark its first appearance here, Robertson calling it a remarkable expression with a modern literature of its own and quoting the judgment that it means much for a speaker who chose it deliberately out of private reflections we can only guess at. Clarke derives it from a Hebrew idiom of humiliation, which is why the meek and lowly Jesus applied it to himself, and thinks it also points to the incarnation as the prophets had predicted it; Wesley traces it to Daniel and to the same humility. Clarke then turns to the reader directly: a poor man who fears God may take comfort in resembling his Lord so nearly, where the rich votary of pleasure is unlike this heavenly pattern altogether.

The fathers take the two creatures for something other than animals. Augustine turns the whole sentence on the hearer: the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head, that is, in your faith; the foxes have holes in your heart, because you are deceitful, and the birds nests there, because you are proud — so the deceitful and the proud are told not to follow, guile being no fit follower of sincerity. Gregory makes the distinction from the creatures’ habits, the fox being crafty, hiding in ditches and dens and never going straight when it comes abroad but in crooked windings, while birds lift themselves into the air; so the foxes are the subtle and deceitful demons and the birds the proud ones, which lodge in such a heart where his own lowliness can find no rest. Rabanus varies the pairing, making the foxes heretics who trust in their own cleverness and the birds the evil spirits, both of them housed in the heart of the Jewish people.
21:
Who the second applicant was cannot be settled, and the attempts are instructive. Gill holds that calling him one of the disciples does not make the scribe one too, thinks he may even have been one of the Twelve, reports that an ancient tradition and one version name him Philip, and reasons that he cannot have been of the seventy, who were not called until later. Ellicott traces the Philip tradition to Clement of Alexandria and will not have it, since nothing in the Gospels suggests it and Philip had been called and had obeyed already; all he will allow is that it may have been so, and that such a man might at this stage have shrunk from the fresh activity of actual service. Barnes and Clarke both pull the word the other way: a disciple is properly a learner, the name belonged to everyone who professed to believe, and it implies no piety at all, only attendance on the teaching for whatever reason.

Whether the father was dead is the real question. Robertson doubts it, contrasts the enthusiast who went before with this over-cautious man, and reads the request as meaning that once his father has died and been buried he will be free to follow — citing Tobit’s charge to his son to bury him when he was dead, and the report of an Oriental who said of his future plans, with his father sitting beside him, that he must first bury his father. Wesley agrees that it is not certain the father was dead and supposes the son wished to stay with a very old man until he died. Calvin thinks the same, since the form of words implies the father had but a short time left, and sets the two men’s faults opposite each other: the scribe offered without consideration and imagined an easy life, while this man was held back by the weakness of counting it a hardship to leave his father — though Calvin is careful to say he does not refuse the call, only asks a delay to discharge a duty he owed. Ellicott leaves both readings of the petition open, that the father was already dead and the last honours were what he asked leave for, or that the death was still to come.

Two take the occasion for a rule. Clarke notes the Jewish maxim that a man with a duty to the dead was for that time free of every other precept, and then observes that the children of Adam always run to extremes, some rushing into the ministry without a call and others delaying long after they have received one. Rabanus states the principle the episode illustrates, that lesser goods must sometimes be given up to secure greater ones. Hilary adds a distinction between the two applicants that turns on the form of their words: this man does not ask whether he should follow, believing already that he ought, but prays only to be allowed to bury his father first.
22:
The paradox is explained the same way by everyone, from a usage. Barnes sets out the two senses of the word and calls the saying a paradox fitted to convey the thought sharply, noting that the Jews often used dead to express indifference, or rather the absence of any influence, as when a man is said to be dead to the world or to the law or to sin, meaning that these have no control over him and are to him as though they were not. Clarke supplies the narrower Jewish usage, that a man who had departed from the precepts of the Law was reckoned dead and every transgressor accounted a dead man, so that the sentence held nothing difficult for a Jew; and he states the distinction plainly, natural death being the separation of body and soul and spiritual death the separation of God and the soul, so that the spiritually dead are left to bury their natural dead. Ellicott calls the saying half epigram and half proverb and paraphrases it as a division of labour: let those with no spiritual life linger in the circle of outward routine, while those who are really alive do the work their Master calls them to and leave the conventional duties to be done or not as events order. Robertson puts it in a sentence, that the spiritually dead are always on hand to bury the physically dead when a man’s real duty lies with Jesus, and quotes Chrysostom to the effect that burying the dead is a good deed and preaching Christ a better.

What the rebuke does not mean is guarded as carefully. Calvin denies outright that burial is condemned here, since to throw bodies away unburied would be shameful and cruel, the custom began in a divine command, and the saints practised it to strengthen the hope of the resurrection; the point is only that whatever draws us off the right course, or holds us back in it, deserves to be called by the name used here — those alone living who give all their thoughts and every part of life to obedience, and those dead who never rise above the world and forget God in pleasing men. Gill reads the command as a refusal to excuse, Christ insisting on the ministry he had called the man to, partly to show that he must be regarded above the nearest relation, partly for the dignity of that ministry above any such service, and partly to signify how little the traditions of the elders weighed with him. Clarke makes the same comparison by office, that any man may perform the common duties of life where the preaching of the kingdom is granted to few. Wesley compresses the whole into a line, that when God calls, the business of the world is to be left to those who are dead to God. Gregory extends the phrase in another direction, that the dead bury the dead whenever sinners shelter sinners, and that those who exalt sinners with their praises hide the dead under a pile of words.
23:
The boat and the company are identified first. Gill has it made ready or hired by the disciples on the orders already given; Barnes supposes a small open sailing boat of the kind used for fishing on the lake, and takes the disciples to include more than the apostles, noting from Mark that other vessels were in company, which makes the miracle the more impressive. Ellicott prefers the better reading, the boat, one belonging perhaps to Peter or the sons of Zebedee and always kept at their Master’s service, and finds in Mark’s phrase that they took him even as he was a sign of extreme exhaustion after teaching, followed at once by sleep in the stern with the boat’s cushion for a pillow. He notes too that Mark and Luke place this and what follows after the parables of the thirteenth chapter. Chrysostom answers that objection directly: Luke frees himself from the order of time by saying it came to pass on a certain day, and Mark does the same, where this Evangelist keeps the order — the writers not all proceeding alike, which is worth saying lest an omission be mistaken for a discordance.

Why he went by sea at all is answered from the purpose of the voyage. Henry recalls the sailing orders for the country of Gadara east of Jordan, where he meant to rescue a man possessed by a legion though he foresaw the affront he would meet there; and observes that the land route would not have been much longer, so that the crossing was chosen to give occasion for showing himself God of the sea as well as of the dry land. Pseudo-Origen puts the same thought as a progression, that having done great things on land he passes to the water to show his power there too and present himself as Lord of both. Chrysostom gives two lessons for which the disciples were taken aboard, not to be confounded in dangers and not to think highly of themselves for being kept when the rest were sent away — which is why he lets them be tossed; and he draws the distinction that where miracles were to be shown the crowd was admitted, but where fears were to be stilled only the victors of the world went along, being men he meant to train for conflict. Calvin spends his space on the geography instead, arguing from Strabo that the Gadarene water was so pestilential that cattle drinking it lost hair and hoofs, where Gennesareth was wholesome, so that two separate lakes must be meant.

The voyage is also read as a figure. Pseudo-Origen holds that the disciples followed as men strong and established in the faith, accompanying him in holiness of spirit rather than merely treading where he trod. Rabanus makes the sea the turmoil of the world and the boat the tree of the cross, by whose help the faithful cross the waves and reach their heavenly country as a safe shore; and he carries the figure into history, so that when Christ was fixed on the cross a great commotion rose, the disciples’ minds being troubled at the passion, and the boat was covered because the whole strength of persecution gathered about that cross. Bede states the simpler version, that the boat is the present Church in which Christ crosses the sea of this world with his own and stills the waves of persecution.
24:
What kind of storm it was is described with some precision. Gill calls it a shaking of the sea, the wind moving the water and both together shaking the vessel and the men in it, and notes that the word Mark and Luke use means a wind whirled suddenly upwards and downwards, or rather a conflict of several winds, so that a whirlwind or hurricane is meant. Robertson agrees on the whirlwind and furious gusts, and explains the cause from the ground: the lake lies six hundred and eighty feet below the Mediterranean, and squalls come down off the summit of Hermon with the force of an earthquake. Ellicott says such storms are common on any inland sea, the wind sweeping through narrow mountain valleys so that water smooth as glass a few minutes before is suddenly white with foaming crests; the boat lay in the trough and shipped the waves until it was filling. Barnes adds that the lake was subject to sudden squalls and that the vessel was fast filling and in danger of sinking.

What raised it is a flat disagreement. Clarke supposes Satan, the prince of the power of the air, excited the tempest, having got the author of the Gospel and all its preachers together in one small vessel and thinking to defeat the purposes of God by drowning it, which must have looked a noble opportunity to the enemy of the human race. Gill denies both chance and Satan outright and assigns the storm to divine providence, raised for the trial of the disciples’ faith. Pseudo-Origen takes Gill’s side and goes further, that the tempest did not arise of itself but in obedience to the power of the one who caused it, which is why it began only after he had embarked; and Chrysostom treats the tossing as something he suffered to happen for their training.

The sleep draws most of the comment. Barnes places him on the hinder part of the vessel on a pillow, supposes it night and the man weary, and makes the calm of it a demonstration to the disciples of how quietly one may sleep with a pure conscience and in the hands of God. Ellicott ends his account on the same contrast, the boat filling with water and still he slept. Jerome finds the type of it in Jonah, who is unconcerned while everyone else is in danger, sleeps, and is woken. Hilary turns the sleep inward, that Christ is cast asleep in us by our own sloth, and that this happens so that in the fear of danger we may hope for help from God, a hope which, though late, may still be confident of escaping by the might of the Christ who watches within. Wesley reduces the whole verse to a proverb, that a man’s extremity is God’s opportunity.
25:
Whether the cry was a prayer or a complaint is the question the verse raises. Barnes takes it straightforwardly as great confidence in the Saviour, and makes it the model for anyone who feels himself in danger of perishing, since none but the Son of God can save from the storms of divine wrath. Robertson renders the Greek more exactly as a plea to be saved at once while they are in the act of perishing. Ellicott hears something less creditable in it, and more of it in Mark, where they ask whether he does not care that they perish: they had begun to think him indifferent to their safety, and perhaps, supposing his own life charmed, were half angry at the indifference. Calvin states the difficulty at its sharpest. On the face of it the prayer is a good and holy one, for what else had men who were lost to do but beg safety of Christ? Yet he charges them with unbelief, so we must ask where the sin lay; and Calvin finds it in their attaching too much weight to his bodily presence, since by Mark they do not merely pray but expostulate, and Luke adds their confusion and trembling. They ought to have known that his Divinity was not overcome by a carnal sleep, and it was to that Divinity they should have had recourse.

Gill places them coming to him from another part of the ship in great consternation. Clarke, meanwhile, spends his note on a single pronoun: the printed editions and the English give his disciples, where the best manuscripts and three named critics omit the possessive. He concedes at once that the point is of very small importance and need not have been raised, and then defends having raised it on principle, that a translator or commentator should render every particle of the inspired writer’s language that can be rendered, and insert no word he has reason to think was not given by inspiration. On the prayer itself he has more to say, following Quesnel: one advantage of trials is to teach us our own weakness and so oblige us to have recourse to God by faith in Christ, since it is by faith that we approach him, by love that we are united to him, and by prayer that we awake him. All good perishes in us without Christ, and without his grace there is no moment in which we are not in danger of utter ruin — which makes this short prayer a familiar one, comprehending as it does the whole power of his might, the merit of his atonement, and the depth of our own danger.
26:
The rebuke is measured before the miracle. Gill allows they had some faith but finds a great deal of fear and unbelief mixed with it, which is what Christ blames. Barnes turns it into a reproach with a reason: they should have remembered who was on board and that he had power to save, and he extends it to all Christians, who are as safe as their Master is and need fear neither danger nor disease nor death. Ellicott notes that Luke sharpens the question to where their faith had gone, as though it had all drifted away under the pressure of fear, and then defends the gentler word used here as singularly apt: they had not wholly lost their trust, but they had not learnt the centurion’s lesson, and were only at ease while they could hear his voice and see him watching them. Clarke draws the contrast as an aphorism, that faith is bold and incredulity timid, and that when faith fails under temptation shipwreck is near — whence the prayer for an increase of it. Wesley sets the two halves of the verse in order, that he composed their spirits first and the sea afterwards.

Why the wind is addressed and not the water is a point Clarke presses. Since the agitation of the sea was only an effect of the wind, the cause had to be removed for the effect to cease, exactly as Joshua did not command the earth to stand still, the earth not being the cause of its own motion, but the sun. Barnes stands on the bare power instead, that the word awed the tempest and allayed the storm, which he takes for irresistible proof of divinity and calls as sublime a description of a display of power as exists anywhere. Ellicott observes that rebuking was almost our Lord’s regular form in working miracles, the fever and the frenzy of the demoniac being rebuked as the tempest is. Calvin takes up the command to be silent that Mark reports and guards it against absurdity: the lake had no perception, and the address was meant to show that the power of his voice reached even senseless elements. He then widens it, that not only things without feeling but obstinate men obey God’s commands — for when God is pleased to quiet the tumults of war he does not always soften fierce minds into obedience but makes the weapons drop from their hands while the rage continues.
27:
Who marvelled is disputed.
