Gill reports that the other two evangelists seem to refer the wonder to the disciples where this one ascribes it to the men, by whom he understands the mariners aboard, and concludes it had the same effect on both, since both were abundantly convinced of his deity and dignity; he gathers from Mark and Luke that the astonishment was mixed with fear or reverence, there being such a shine of majesty in the business. Ellicott reasons from the vagueness of the word men, which is so exceptional as applied to the disciples that he suspects others were in the boat. Calvin weighs both readings and prefers the second, that the speakers were men who had not yet come to know Christ, since Mark and Luke report the apostles crying out in fear after the reproof; and he adds that the result of the miracle is the same display of Christ’s glory whichever view is taken.

The question itself is read as a confession. Barnes paraphrases it as asking what personage this can be, how unlike other men, how far exalted above mortals — and sets the scene against itself, the storm subsiding, the ship gliding smoothly, the danger gone, and the men standing in amazement before one who controlled the tempests God had raised, until they felt that he must be God himself, since none but God could calm such billows. Clarke renders the phrase as how great is this person and answers it the same way, that here was God fully manifest, but manifest in the flesh, where his power lay hidden. The Gloss quotes Chrysostom for the neatest division of the evidence: the sleeping and the appearance showed the man, the sea and the calm pointed out the God. Clarke adds a moral from the obedience of the elements, that every part of creation except man hears and obeys its Creator’s voice, while sinners keep an ear for the world and the devil and the flesh, and until that ear is shut to his enemies God’s voice goes undiscerned.

Two further observations stand at the edges. Robertson insists on calling it a nature miracle and disposes of an evasion: even a sudden drop in the wind would not at once calm a sea, and of the suggestion that by an astonishing coincidence the storm happened to lull at the moment Christ spoke he remarks only that some minds are easily satisfied by their own stupidities. Ellicott, at the other end, grants that the spiritual application of the story lies so near the surface that it has become a commonplace of sermons and hymns, and maintains nevertheless that there is a fitness in it which never stops being fresh, the elements seeming further from human control than leprosy or fever and proving as subject to his sovereignty.
28:
The place-name is the first tangle, and nobody pretends otherwise. Clarke lists five spellings across the manuscripts and versions, holds the first three best attested, and cites Origen against identifying these people with the inhabitants of Gerasa, a city of Arabia with neither sea nor lake near it; from Josephus he gives Gadara as the metropolis of the region beyond Jordan. Barnes calls the difference only apparent, Gadara standing near the lake among the ten cities and Gergesa some twelve miles to its south-east and twenty east of Jordan, so that each writer named a different town of the same district. Robertson settles it from the ground, reporting ruins found beside the lake in Gadara’s territory, which makes either name usable. Wesley says the same more plainly, that the country between two neighbouring towns took its name now from one and now from the other. Lightfoot accepts both readings, Gadara giving the district its name and Gergasa being a town inside it. Ellicott, who spends longest on it, grants the locality is hard to determine and describes Gadara as sixteen miles from Tiberias, identified now with ruins over two miles round at the north-west end of the mountains of Gilead.

Whether there were one sufferer or two is the second. Chrysostom explains that the other two evangelists chose the more grievously afflicted man, which is why they add particulars, the broken bonds and the desert in one, the cutting with stones in the other; and he notes that neither of them says there was only one, which alone would make a contradiction. Augustine supposes one of them a man of note, whose condition the whole country grieved over and whose recovery was much cared about, so that the fame of the cure spread the wider. Calvin treats the whole doubt as settled already, since the country is the one Luke expressly places opposite Galilee and every circumstance agrees, so that events coinciding at all points cannot have happened at different times; the single difference of number is what misled commentators.

The tombs and the fierceness are read both literally and figuratively. Robertson describes the chambers cut into the hillside, common in that country then and now, the eastern cliffs being limestone and full of caves. Wesley places tombs in desert spots at a distance from towns, often cut in the sides of caves, and thinks such tokens of death and destruction are what those malevolent spirits love. Lightfoot quotes the rabbinic marks of a madman, that he goes out at night and lodges among the sepulchres. Rabanus finds the dwelling significant, asking what the bodies of the faithless are but sepulchres of the dead, where the word of God does not live; and he reads the name of the place as casting out the dweller, or a stranger approaching, applied to the Gentile world that cast the Devil out. Ambrose makes the pair themselves a type of the Gentiles, since of Noah’s three sons only one line was taken into God’s inheritance and the nations sprang from the other two. Hilary puts them outside the town, which is to say outside the synagogue of the Law and the Prophets, infesting the ancient seats of the two nations, their coming out to meet him standing for men flocking to the faith. Chrysostom gives the reason the demons spoke at all: since some took Christ for a man, they came to proclaim his divinity, so that those who had not seen the sea raging and then still might at least hear the demons cry out. Henry sets the episode at the head of the chapter’s argument, that its scope is to show the divine power of Christ over diseases, then over winds and waves, and last over devils, which are the most formidable of all, since he holds not only all power in heaven and earth but the keys of hell.
29:
The idiom is translated three ways. Barnes thinks it would be better rendered as asking what Christ has to do with them, the sense being why he should trouble or disturb them, and cites Old Testament parallels. Clarke gives it literally as what is it to us and to thee, suspects it may disclaim any intention of interfering with his work and ask the same forbearance in return, and calls the phrase a Jewish one recurring in the Old Testament for an abrupt refusal or a wish not to be troubled, instancing Jehu’s retort to Joram’s messenger. Remigius reads a doctrine out of it instead, that their malice and his grace have nothing in common. Gill keeps to the force of the scene: devils who had made these men so outrageous no one could pass the road cried out at the sight of him in consternation and utter subjection.

Whether they knew what they were saying is the real dispute. Robertson finds the recognition surprising, grants that the whole subject is difficult, and rejects the view that possession is merely an old way of describing disease, since that will not explain this scene, where the demons are treated as real existences distinct from the human person; he adds that the devil knew Christ plainly, so that recognition by the devil’s agents is no wonder. Jerome denies it was a confession at all, or at least a voluntary one: it was extorted by necessity, as a runaway slave who meets his master after long absence thinks first of begging off the scourge, these demons supposing from his sudden appearance on earth that he had come to judge them. He rejects as absurd the notion that the demons knew the Son of God while the Devil did not, on the ground that their lesser wickedness made them wiser, since whatever the disciple knows must be granted to the master; his own verdict is that Devil and demons alike suspected rather than knew. Pseudo-Augustine argues the same from Paul, that had they known him they would never have let the Lord of glory be crucified. Remigius allows them an oscillating opinion, reckoning him Son of God whenever his power tormented them or they saw him work signs, and doubting when they saw him hungry and thirsty and taking him for a mere man; and he turns the confession against two parties, the Jews who said he cast out devils by Beelzebub and the Arians who called him a creature, both condemned on the demons’ own testimony. Augustine states the limit precisely, that God was known to them only so far as it pleased him to be known and as far as was needful — not as he is eternal Life and the Light that enlightens the good, but by temporal effects of his excellence and signs of a hidden presence such as angelic spirits can see.

The last clause and the restraint behind it close the comment. Wesley glosses the time as the great day. Robertson notes that what they fear is torment before it, and that they know nothing is common between them and the Son of God. Calvin reads the whole cry as an attempt to drive him off which turns into complaint and entreaty once they find themselves held and his authority not to be declined; from which he draws the character of devils, that they breathe nothing but rebellion and yet for all their swelling pride are crushed in a moment, a malice never subdued still struggling against God’s government and still compelled to yield. He observes too that Christ does not here openly reject the devil’s confession as he did elsewhere. Gregory supplies the ground of the restraint, that the Devil knows he has no power of himself to do anything, since he does not of himself exist as a spirit.
30:
How near the herd was is read off the three accounts. Gill reconciles them: Mark has it nigh unto the mountains and Luke on the mountain, bordering the shore, so that it was at some distance yet within sight, while the Latin and two other versions give not far off or near them, which agrees with the other evangelists placing the swine hard by. Barnes notes that the word now kept for cattle formerly covered any collection of beasts, or even of men, and supplies the number from Mark, two thousand.

How swine came to be there at all is the question the verse raises, and the answers divide along a single line. Gill asks it directly, since the flesh was forbidden the Jews to eat, and so does Ellicott, who answers it from the garrison: the Jews did not eat pork but Roman soldiers did, and the herd may have been kept to supply the legion the possessed man knew by name, with the emperor’s pun about Herod’s swine and his son suggesting that the king kept them on his estates for the same purpose. Clarke takes the opposite view, that the animals were in all probability Jewish property kept in express violation of the law of God, so that their destruction was nothing more than a proper manifestation of his justice. Wesley says the same in a line, that keeping them was unlawful for Jews and their loss was therefore both just and merciful. Lightfoot poses the alternative as a question — whether these Gadarenes were Jews or heathens — and assembles the Jewish evidence: that keeping swine was a matter of infamy, witness the rabbi whose red face led a woman to guess him a winebibber, a usurer or a keeper of hogs; and that the wise men forbade keeping hogs anywhere, and a dog unless it were chained, partly for the damage such animals did in other men’s fields, the keeping of smaller cattle being generally forbidden in the land of Israel.

Bede alone reads the herd figuratively, making the swine those who delight in filthy manners, since unless a man lives as a swine the devils receive no power over him, and at most a power to try him rather than to destroy.
31:
What the demons were asking to avoid is supplied from the other Gospels. Ellicott gives Mark’s form, that he should not send them out of the district they were in, and Luke’s, that he should not command them into the deep, which he identifies with the abyss of the Revelation; the man speaks as the demons speak, identifying himself with them, and what he shrinks from is wandering in dry places seeking rest and finding none, or being driven like Asmodeus to the ends of Egypt, or worst of all being shut in the abyss. Gill has the whole legion of them perceiving they must come out and begging hard after their first plea failed, their motive being that they had been long in that country and had made themselves masters of the tempers and circumstances of its people, and could therefore do the more mischief where they were.

Why they asked for the swine in particular is where Calvin parts from the obvious answer. Some conjecture it was mere enmity to God’s creatures, and he grants they are wholly bent on overthrowing the order God appointed in nature; but he is certain of a remoter aim, to provoke the people of the country into cursing God over the loss. The parallel he offers is Job, where the devil brings down the house not from any hatred of timber or stones but so that a good man, losing patience under loss, may break out against God.

Clarke works on the verb. The common text has them ask leave to go, but he judges the better attested reading to be that he should send them, a reading he says Griesbach adopted on the authority of three ancient manuscripts and a long list of versions; and he prefers it for its sense, since being sent expresses the absolute power Christ held over them more fully than being permitted — bare leave would not have been enough, the very power by which they went having to come from him. On which Clarke remarks how empty the boast of Satan in the wilderness looks beside a spirit that cannot enter so much as the body of a beast without being sent.
32:
The single word of consent is weighed carefully. Wesley insists it is permission only and not command. Gill reasons the same way and draws the comfort out of it: the leave given here is the leave God gave Satan in the case of Job, and since without divine permission these spirits can do nothing to the bodies or souls or estates of men — could not so much as enter swine unasked, much less anything greater — they are not to be dreaded, least of all by the people of God. Ellicott faces the scorn the verse attracts, that the word was needless and the destruction fruitless, and refuses the rationalising escape by which the demoniacs themselves stampeded the herd, since even if that were tenable on other grounds the words plainly sanctioned what followed; his own suggestion is that only some such visible separation could deliver the man from the inextricable confusion between himself and the unclean spirits he had been caught in. Clarke notes the oddity that a prayer of demons was heard at all, and answers that God hears demons, and certain men, only when their prayer happens to echo his own justice.

The rush down the cliff is reported and then interpreted. Robertson places it as a plunge from the cliff into the lake and states the chain of mastery he finds in it, the mind of the Master over the minds of the maniacs and his power over the demons and over the herd; difficulties abound, he grants, for those who see only folk-lore and legend, but the account is plain enough on the assumption that Jesus is really Lord, and the incidental loss of the animals need not trouble readers familiar with natural disasters they cannot explain either. Clarke makes the drowning an emblem of the final impenitence and ruin of swinish sinners. Bede reads it of the Gentile world, that when those nations are delivered from the condemnation of the demons there are still those who will not believe and who keep their profane rites in secret, drowned in a blind and deep curiosity. Hilary has the demons, finding no place left among the Gentiles, asking leave to live among heretics, who are then carried down and drowned in worldly desires at their instigation. Gill raises the practical objection, why Christ should allow a loss so considerable to the owners, and answers it by the ownership — if they were Jews, the herd should not have been there at all.
33:
Who the herdsmen were, and why they ran, is read from their trade. Gill calls them men of very low life in an employment reckoned infamous, and gives three reasons at once for the flight: amazement at what they had seen, distress at losing the swine and with them their living, and fear of being blamed by their masters. Clarke says only that they were terrified at what had happened to the herd.

Barnes uses the verse to settle the ownership question the chapter keeps raising. The swine belonged to the people of Gadara, and whether those were Jews or Gentiles cannot be known for certain; the district was not properly within Judaea but lay on its border, so the population was probably mixed. Since swine were unclean to Jews, who were forbidden not only to eat them but by their own law to keep them even for trade, the alternative is strict: either the owners had plainly broken the law, or the herd was Gentile property. He guesses at their motive too: either they feared a further destruction of property, or, more likely, knowing the Jewish law, they took the loss for a judgment of Heaven on men who kept forbidden animals and tempted their neighbours to break God’s commands.

Barnes then turns the episode into a defence of the whole narrative against objectors who call it a wanton violation of private rights, or simply ridiculous. He answers in three steps. If Christ is divine, the property was his already and he might dispose of it as he pleased; nobody complains when God destroys far more by earthquake or pestilence or lightning, and there is no reason to complain because the same thing is done another way. If the herd was Jewish it was held against their own law and the loss was deserved; if Gentile, it was a snare and an abomination to the people among whom they lived, and the nuisance was rightly removed. And the cure of two men, one of them probably a person of standing, was worth more than the animals. He adds an observation about the miracles at large: this and the cursing of the fig-tree are the only two that destroyed any property, which he reads as proof of benevolence, since the divine mission might have been confirmed just as well by splitting rocks or moving mountains or making water run up a hill, and was confirmed instead in ways that did men good.

Bede alone takes the errand allegorically, making the flight and the report a figure of the leaders of the wicked, who shun the law of Christianity and yet do not cease to publish the wonderful power of Christ.
34:
Why the crowd came out at all is guessed at, and the guesses are unflattering. Gill reads the whole city as the greater part of its inhabitants rather than every soul, and adds from Luke that the multitude came from the surrounding country too, the news having gone into both. Barnes supposes they set out meaning to arrest him for the damage to their property and were awed into asking only that he go. Clarke puts it more bluntly, that they probably came intending to destroy him for destroying their swine, and were checked by the sight of him into merely begging him off their borders. Ellicott finds the request characteristic of a wild, half-heathen population, who could look at a prophet who had done so great a work and see a Destroyer rather than a Saviour, and so shrink from having him among them.

What the request reveals is where the comment presses hardest, and it presses in one direction. Barnes draws two lessons: that Satan’s design is to prejudice men against the Saviour, even to the point of making what Christ does the reason they want him gone; and that this is the power of avarice, since these men preferred their property to him and loved it enough to go blind both to the evidence of the miracle and to the good done to the wretched men who had been healed. Clarke says the same of men who would rather lose Christ than the temporal goods by which they gratify their passions at their souls’ expense, and concludes that they loved their swine better than their salvation. Robertson and Wesley both end on that note, Robertson that a city excited about dead hogs had forgotten the healing of the demoniacs altogether and cared more for the animals than for human souls, Wesley that many are still of the same mind. Ellicott sets the one exception against them, the healed man himself, whose faith was real if weak.

Two further details stand apart from the reproach. Ellicott supplies what the other Gospels add, that they found the man clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus in the clinging gratitude of faith, and suggests that the garment which was now the outward sign of a new self-respect had been given him out of the disciples’ pity. Clarke, meanwhile, turns on the scholars who explain the whole episode away. Doctors in both divinity and physic, he says, gravely assure us that these men were only common madmen and that superstitious Jews attributed the disease to demons; and with all deference to great characters he asks by what figure of speech two diseases can be said to have besought, and gone out, and filled a herd of swine, and rushed down a precipice. Robertson meets the same evasion from the other end of the story, allowing that difficulties remain for anyone who sees only folk-lore here.
